findings.title: Denial cache key collides with the permission cache key
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey builds `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>`. userPermCacheKey builds `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>`. Both use the same `perm_` prefix and the same underlying cache. The two keys differ only by the extra `_name_parent` suffix. A user UID or action containing underscores could make the two keys equal, and the cached types differ (bool vs map). Separators are also unescaped, so name/parent pairs can collide. For example, name `a_b` with parent `c` and name `a` with parent `b_c` produce the same key. A distinct prefix such as `perm_denial_` and a safer delimiter would avoid both problems.

findings.title: Denial cache defeats the purpose of re-querying for newly created resources
findings.body: A denial is cached for 30s after the DB re-query. Suppose a user checks a resource before permissions are granted, for example a folder or dashboard being created. The denial is then cached, and the creator is denied for up to 30s after creation. This is the scenario the PR is meant to fix. Denials are also never invalidated when permissions change. The cache fixes the extra-DB-load problem but reintroduces a delay.

findings.title: Cached-permission lookup errors are silently ignored
findings.body: getCachedIdentityPermissions can fail on GetUserIdentifiers, which may hit the DB. The error is swallowed and execution falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which repeats the same lookup. On failure this means a redundant DB call. The permissionCacheUsage metric is also recorded as a miss even though the cause was an error rather than a cache miss.
